title: The AI Era Should Be Led by HR, Not IT: Hire AI Like an Employee
dek: Treating AI as a technology purchase handed to IT is serving the main course as a side dish; what actually needs to be broken apart is tasks, not jobs, and HR should lead it, because AI has no feelings and people do.
why: Medium information density, but the two mechanisms — "hiring AI as talent" and "intelligence lock-in" — plus a few concrete numbers are worth hearing; the rest is mostly experiential.
who: HR leaders, COOs and business-line managers pushing AI adoption, especially companies that treat AI as a technology purchase handed to IT.
skip: The 1:02:46 to 1:05:48 segment on what small companies should do — mostly experiential.

points.h: Every company in the information business lands in the top-right quadrant
points.body: Mike used Replit to build a tool in one night (8pm to 8am), fed it employment research from roughly 15 think tanks and research institutions worldwide, ranked them across four quadrants from least likely to be disrupted to most likely, and looked up only one company — One Digital. It landed in the most disruptable quadrant, a blinking red dot, flagging that about 25% of roles could be disrupted by AI. His conclusion: any company in the information business will land in that top-right quadrant.

points.h: What should be broken apart is tasks, not jobs
points.body: Mike thinks everyone is looking at the problem through the wrong lens — "jobs" — when what really needs to be broken apart are the tasks that make up each job: everyone has a pre-AI job description, and almost certainly a post-AI job description too. They call this mapping the work genome, are piloting it with four teams, and are bringing in three academic institutions to add rigor. His worry: cutting first and thinking about downstream later is the easier path, and many companies will take it.

points.h: HR, not IT, should lead this
points.body: Mike is blunt: the group that should be driving this is not the IT department but the HR team. Over the past hundred years HR went from a payroll administrative function to being elevated into the executive suite in the 80s and 90s because talent was the source of intellectual property; now it needs to rise another level — managing not human talent but the organization's human plus AI talent. The reason isn't that AI matters, it's that AI has no feelings and doesn't need to support a family, while talent does, so the people assigned to care about people should lead it.

They split human work into reducible and irreducible. Reducible is what can be broken into processes, with clear steps, handed to AI, and AI only gets better at it; irreducible is the "squishy" part — you can't explain how it works but it just does, coming from experience, life, and signals received from the environment. The key judgment: irreducible skills have no ceiling, and the time saved should be invested on that side. In wealth management, for example, investment modeling, information synthesis and preparing client meeting materials are things AI does increasingly well; what's irreducible is the human judgment that connects information to a client's real desires.

points.h: AI employees have résumés, and PIPs too
points.body: One Digital "hires" AI as talent: AI colleagues have job titles, job descriptions, even résumés, all managed by human supervisors, going through a full HR process, and some AI colleagues have even been put on a PIP (performance improvement plan). Vinay says this isn't buying technology, it's "hire the AI into the organization." The direct consequence: when both AI and humans are doing the work, the real question becomes "what is the optimal ratio of human to AI on this task," and that ratio is constantly shifting at both ends — what AI can do is changing, and so is what humans can do. The workforce intelligence score exists to quantify and iterate on this.

points.h: Answer engine and collaborative relationship are two different uses
points.body: Vinay splits AI use into two types. One is transactional: treating AI as an answer engine, as an errand runner — "write that email I don't want to write to my kid's teacher," "read this document that's too long." This use simultaneously underestimates AI and yourself. The other is collaborative: you and AI talk, brainstorm, share a goal and push it forward together. One Digital has hundreds of thousands of chat records between employees and AI colleagues, now analyzed by another set of AI colleagues, which can identify when a person shifts from transactional to collaborative — this "amplification score" is the computational driver of the workforce intelligence score.

points.h: The risk of intelligence lock-in is no less than data lock-in
points.body: Vinay opposes companies signing one blanket agreement with Anthropic or OpenAI and having everyone use Claude or ChatGPT. His reasoning: the business these companies want is "renting intelligence to you," so they may raise the rent on intelligence the way a landlord does, and may say "unless you give me X, Y, Z, you don't get the smartest intelligence." A few years from now, when humans work alongside AI every day and the organization's shared intelligence lives between people and AI, that company has you by the throat. When people talk about vendor lock-in they mean data locked in a CRM; intelligence lock-in will be a different problem. The solution is owning your own intelligence: being able to hand-pick models per task, not going to a large model for things a small, cheap model can do well, which also optimizes spend.

points.h: Writing software will become like using a spreadsheet
points.body: Vinay thinks engineering is no longer "the longest pole in the tent," no longer a special skill held by a small group of prima donnas who need to be protected and paid top dollar — AI can already write software. If AI can write software, the question becomes: how do you build a governance framework so technology development spreads through the organization and captures the innovation happening among employees. He predicts writing software will become as common as using a spreadsheet: some people are great at Excel, some aren't, but everyone uses spreadsheets. He also flags the need for governance — they lived through "spreadsheet hell," where determining whether a family trust was suitable ended up spawning six different Excel files, and it took years to get back to a single tool. The good news is AI can help with governance too, like reading code and finding two people doing the same thing, then merging them directly.

points.h: If the CEO isn't lit up, the whole company won't change
points.body: Vinay says one pattern in their data is very hard: if a manager is activated and has a high AI amplification score, their team follows immediately. So his blunt advice to listeners is — if your CEO or boss hasn't had that "oh moment," your organization won't change. It's not enough to say "I believe in AI, we deployed AI": a CEO can't write about AI in the shareholder letter while doing their own job the way they did for the past thirty years. They have to actually change their own work, because that flows downward, gives employees permission, removes fear, and makes using AI no longer a stigma.
